coverage: Dedication, all 26 chapters and their surviving editorial notes in both English editions. Historical, religious, literary and editorial references, named families and specific ruler roles. Generic princes, offices and population names are not automatically individual people.

entities.name: Lorenzo de’ Medici
entities.body: Lorenzo di Piero de’ Medici, the young Florentine ruler to whom Machiavelli dedicates the book.

entities.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
entities.body: The Florentine diplomat and author of this advice on political power.

entities.name: Francesco Sforza
entities.body: The military commander who became Duke of Milan; Lodovico’s father.

entities.name: Ferdinand of Aragon
entities.body: Ferdinand II of Aragon, the Spanish king repeatedly used as an example of political strategy.

entities.name: Pope Julius II
entities.body: Giuliano della Rovere, the pope whose military and political campaigns Machiavelli examines.
aliases: Cardinal of San Pietro ad Vincula

entities.name: Louis XII
entities.body: The French king whose attempts to hold territory in Italy Machiavelli analyzes.

entities.name: Lodovico Sforza
entities.body: The Duke of Milan known as Lodovico Moro; Francesco Sforza’s son and Beatrice d’Este’s husband.

entities.name: Beatrice d’Este
entities.body: Lodovico Sforza’s wife, the duchess of Milan.

entities.name: Antiochus III
entities.body: The Seleucid king whose intervention in Greece brought him into conflict with Rome.

entities.name: Philip V of Macedon
entities.body: The Macedonian king who fought Rome and was defeated by Flamininus.

entities.name: Philip II of Macedon
entities.body: Alexander the Great’s father, the Macedonian king cited on military power.

entities.name: Charles VIII
entities.body: The French king whose invasion of Italy preceded the campaigns of Louis XII.

entities.name: Pope Alexander VI
entities.body: Rodrigo Borgia, the pope and father of Cesare Borgia.

entities.name: Jeanne of France
entities.body: Louis XII’s first wife and Louis XI’s daughter.

entities.name: Louis XI
entities.body: The French king who was Charles VII’s son and Jeanne’s father.

entities.name: Anne of Brittany
entities.body: The duchess of Brittany who married Charles VIII and later Louis XII.

entities.name: Georges d’Amboise
entities.body: The French cardinal and archbishop of Rouen, an adviser to Louis XII.

entities.name: Cesare Borgia
entities.body: Pope Alexander VI’s son, the military ruler also called Duke Valentino.

entities.name: Alexander the Great
entities.body: The Macedonian conqueror and son of Philip II.

entities.name: Darius III
entities.body: The Persian king whose empire Alexander the Great conquered.

entities.name: Darius I
entities.body: The Persian king cited for installing dependent rulers in Greek territories.

entities.name: Pyrrhus
entities.body: The king of Epirus cited in the discussion of holding conquered territory.

entities.name: Cyrus the Great
entities.body: The founder of the Persian Empire, used as a model of a ruler who establishes a new state.

entities.name: Girolamo Savonarola
entities.body: The Florentine friar and religious reformer cited as an unarmed prophet.

entities.name: Hiero II
entities.body: The ruler of Syracuse used as an example of building power through one’s own forces.

entities.name: Bianca Maria Visconti
entities.body: Francesco Sforza’s wife and Filippo Maria Visconti’s daughter.

entities.name: Filippo Maria Visconti
entities.body: The Duke of Milan whose daughter Bianca Maria married Francesco Sforza.

entities.name: Vitellozzo Vitelli
entities.body: The military commander, brother of Pagolo Vitelli and associate of Oliverotto da Fermo.

entities.name: Paolo Orsini
entities.body: The Orsini commander who mediates the reconciliation with Cesare Borgia; called Signor Pagolo.

entities.name: Ramiro d’Orco
entities.body: Cesare Borgia’s governor in the Romagna, also called Ramiro de Lorqua.

entities.name: Raffaello Riario
entities.body: The cardinal of San Giorgio, named among those injured by Cesare Borgia.

entities.name: Ascanio Sforza
entities.body: The cardinal of the Milanese Sforza family named among Cesare Borgia’s opponents.

entities.name: Giovanni Colonna
entities.body: The Colonna cardinal named among those with grounds to resent Cesare Borgia.

entities.name: Agathocles
entities.body: The ruler of Syracuse used in the discussion of acquiring power through violence.

entities.name: Hamilcar
entities.body: The Carthaginian commander in Sicily with whom Agathocles reaches an understanding.

entities.name: Oliverotto da Fermo
entities.body: The military commander and nephew of Giovanni Fogliani, discussed as a ruler who seizes power violently.

entities.name: Giovanni Fogliani
entities.body: Oliverotto da Fermo’s maternal uncle, who brings him up.

entities.name: Paolo Vitelli
entities.body: The Florentine military commander called Pagolo Vitelli; Vitellozzo’s brother.

entities.name: L. Arthur Burd
entities.body: The editor and commentator on The Prince cited in the translation’s notes.

entities.name: Nabis
entities.body: The ruler of Sparta used in the argument about securing popular support.

entities.name: Giorgio Scali
entities.body: The Florentine political leader cited as an example of misplaced reliance on popular support.

entities.name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus
entities.body: The Roman commander who fought Philip V and Nabis.

entities.name: Pope Sixtus IV
entities.body: The pope cited in the account of papal authority and Rome’s rival baronial families.

entities.name: Pope Leo X
entities.body: Giovanni de’ Medici, the Medici pope reigning when Machiavelli writes.

entities.name: Francis Bacon
entities.body: The English writer whose history of Henry VII is quoted in an editorial note.

entities.name: Henry VII of England
entities.body: The English king who is the subject of Bacon’s history cited in a note.

entities.name: Epaminondas
entities.body: The Theban commander mentioned in the discussion of mercenary armies.

entities.name: Muzio Attendolo Sforza
entities.body: Francesco Sforza’s father, a mercenary captain employed by Joanna II of Naples.

entities.name: Joanna II of Naples
entities.body: The queen of Naples who employs Sforza’s father.

entities.name: Alfonso V of Aragon
entities.body: The Aragonese king to whom Joanna II turns for protection.

entities.name: John Hawkwood
entities.body: The English mercenary commander known in Italy as Giovanni Acuto.

entities.name: Braccio da Montone
entities.body: The mercenary captain whose military following rivals the Sforza commanders.

entities.name: Carmagnola
entities.body: Francesco Bussone, the mercenary commander who serves Milan and Venice.

entities.name: Bartolomeo Colleoni
entities.body: The Venetian commander from Bergamo, named among Venice’s hired captains.

entities.name: Roberto Sanseverino
entities.body: The military commander named among Venice’s hired captains.

entities.name: Niccolò Orsini
entities.body: The Count of Pitigliano, a military commander employed by Venice.

entities.name: Ladislaus of Naples
entities.body: The king of Naples named in the note on Joanna II.

entities.name: Edward III of England
entities.body: The English king mentioned in the note on John Hawkwood.

entities.name: Donnina Visconti
entities.body: John Hawkwood’s wife and Bernabò Visconti’s daughter; called Domnia in the original edition.

entities.name: Bernabò Visconti
entities.body: The ruler of Milan cited for conspicuous rewards and punishments; Donnina’s father.

entities.name: Sigismund of Austria
entities.body: The Habsburg duke named in the note on Roberto Sanseverino’s last campaign.

entities.name: Alberico da Barbiano
entities.body: The mercenary commander who leads the Company of St George; also called Alberigo da Conio.

entities.name: John VI Kantakouzenos
entities.body: The Byzantine emperor cited for bringing Turkish auxiliary troops into Greece.

entities.name: Charles VII
entities.body: The French king cited for establishing his own military forces; Louis XI’s father.

entities.name: Arthur Balfour
entities.body: The British politician quoted in an editorial note on military obligations.

entities.name: Philopoemen
entities.body: The Achaean leader cited for studying military situations even in peacetime.

entities.name: Julius Caesar
entities.body: The Roman general and ruler cited as a model of political and military ambition.

entities.name: Scipio Africanus
entities.body: The Roman commander who defeated Hannibal, cited on military discipline and imitation of Cyrus.

entities.name: Xenophon
entities.body: The Greek writer whose account of Cyrus supplies a model of princely conduct.

entities.name: Virgil
entities.body: The Roman poet quoted through Dido’s speech in the Aeneid.

entities.name: Christopher Pitt
entities.body: The English translator credited for the verse from Virgil.

entities.name: Hannibal
entities.body: The Carthaginian commander cited for maintaining discipline in a diverse army.

entities.name: Fabius Maximus
entities.body: The Roman commander who criticizes Scipio’s leniency.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: The Roman statesman and philosopher whose On Duties is cited in a note.

entities.name: Robert South
entities.body: The English preacher quoted in the note on religion and political appearances.

entities.name: Annibale I Bentivoglio
entities.body: The earlier ruler of Bologna; Giovanni II’s father and Annibale II’s grandfather.

entities.name: Annibale II Bentivoglio
entities.body: The younger Annibale, grandson of the earlier Bolognese ruler.

entities.name: Giovanni II Bentivoglio
entities.body: The ruler of Bologna who is Annibale I’s son and Annibale II’s father.

entities.name: Sante Bentivoglio
entities.body: The Bentivoglio relative raised in Florence who is called to govern Bologna during Giovanni’s childhood.

entities.name: Pietro Paolo Boscoli
entities.body: The Florentine conspirator whose case is mentioned in the note about Machiavelli’s arrest.

entities.name: Marcus Aurelius
entities.body: The Roman emperor and philosopher, father of Commodus.

entities.name: Commodus
entities.body: The Roman emperor who succeeds his father, Marcus Aurelius.

entities.name: Pertinax
entities.body: The Roman emperor who succeeds Commodus, discussed in relation to the army’s power.

entities.name: Didius Julianus
entities.body: The Roman emperor called Julian, who precedes Septimius Severus.

entities.name: Septimius Severus
entities.body: The Roman emperor, father of Caracalla, examined as an example of force and cunning.

entities.name: Caracalla
entities.body: The Roman emperor and son of Septimius Severus, also called Antoninus.

entities.name: Macrinus
entities.body: The Roman emperor who follows Caracalla, included in the survey of imperial rule.

entities.name: Elagabalus
entities.body: The Roman emperor called Heliogabalus in this translation.

entities.name: Severus Alexander
entities.body: The Roman emperor discussed after Elagabalus, distinct from Alexander the Great and Pope Alexander VI.

entities.name: Maximinus Thrax
entities.body: The Roman emperor who rises from the army after Severus Alexander.

entities.name: Pescennius Niger
entities.body: The eastern commander who competes with Septimius Severus for the Roman throne.

entities.name: Clodius Albinus
entities.body: The western commander whose imperial ambitions conflict with those of Septimius Severus.

entities.name: Pandolfo Petrucci
entities.body: The ruler of Siena whose choice of advisers Machiavelli praises.

entities.name: Niccolò Vitelli
entities.body: The ruler of Città di Castello cited for demolishing fortresses.

entities.name: Guidobaldo da Montefeltro
entities.body: The Duke of Urbino cited in the discussion of fortresses.

entities.name: Caterina Sforza
entities.body: The ruler of Forlì, wife of Girolamo Riario; called Catherine Sforza in the notes.

entities.name: Girolamo Riario
entities.body: Caterina Sforza’s husband and co-ruler at Forlì.

entities.name: Galeazzo Maria Sforza
entities.body: The Duke of Milan who is Caterina Sforza’s father.

entities.name: Lucrezia Landriani
entities.body: Caterina Sforza’s mother.

entities.name: Fortunati
entities.body: Caterina Sforza’s correspondent, quoted on Machiavelli’s appointment as envoy.

entities.name: Count Pasolini
entities.body: The author of the biography of Caterina Sforza cited in the notes.

entities.name: P. Sylvester
entities.body: The translator credited for the biography of Caterina Sforza.

entities.name: John Florio
entities.body: The lexicographer quoted on the Italian word for a trade guild.

entities.name: Edgcumbe Staley
entities.body: The writer on Florentine guilds cited in the notes.

entities.name: Donald Mackenzie Wallace
entities.body: The writer whose account of Russian labor associations is quoted in a note.

entities.name: Aylmer Maude
entities.body: The writer consulted in the note on the Russian word artel.

entities.name: Antonio da Venafro
entities.body: Pandolfo Petrucci’s adviser, used as an example of a well-chosen minister.

entities.name: Fra Luca
entities.body: The agent of Emperor Maximilian whose account of the emperor’s indecision Machiavelli reports.

entities.name: Maximilian I
entities.body: The Holy Roman emperor whose way of consulting advisers Machiavelli criticizes.

entities.name: Mary of Burgundy
entities.body: Maximilian I’s first wife and Charles the Bold’s daughter.

entities.name: Charles the Bold
entities.body: The duke of Burgundy whose daughter Mary marries Maximilian I.

entities.name: Bianca Maria Sforza
entities.body: Maximilian I’s second wife, from Milan’s ruling family.

entities.name: Frederick the Great
entities.body: The Prussian king quoted on the power of chance in an editorial note.

entities.name: Albert Sorel
entities.body: The historian whose Eastern Question is cited for the remark attributed to Frederick the Great.

entities.name: Pope Clement VII
entities.body: Giulio de’ Medici, the Medici cardinal identified as Clement VII in the final chapter’s note.

entities.name: Petrarch
entities.body: The Italian poet whose appeal for Italy closes Machiavelli’s exhortation.

entities.name: Edward Dacre
entities.body: The translator credited for the closing lines from Petrarch.

entities.name: Moses
entities.body: The biblical leader of the Israelites, cited as a founder and lawgiver.

entities.name: God
entities.body: The divine authority invoked in the discussions of founders, religion and Italy’s deliverance.

entities.name: Romulus
entities.body: The legendary founder of Rome, used as a model of founding a new state.

entities.name: Theseus
entities.body: The legendary Athenian king credited with uniting Athens.

entities.name: Achilles
entities.body: The Greek hero of the Trojan War, cited as Alexander’s model and Chiron’s pupil.

entities.name: Chiron
entities.body: The centaur who teaches Achilles in Greek legend.

entities.name: Dido
entities.body: The queen of Carthage in Virgil’s Aeneid, quoted on the insecurity of a new reign.

entities.name: David
entities.body: The biblical hero who refuses Saul’s armor before confronting Goliath.

entities.name: Saul
entities.body: The biblical king who offers David his weapons and armor.

entities.name: Goliath
entities.body: The Philistine champion confronted by David in the biblical story.

entities.name: The Este dukes of Ferrara
entities.body: The hereditary dynasty invoked through the attacks of 1484 and 1510, which fall under different dukes.

entities.name: Ercole I d’Este
entities.body: The Duke of Ferrara among the Italian rulers who make advances to Louis XII.

entities.name: The Ottoman sultan
entities.body: The Ottoman ruler, called the Turk, whose centralized government Machiavelli contrasts with France.

entities.name: The Mamluk sultan
entities.body: The ruler of Egypt, called the Soldan, whose power depends on the military elite.

entities.name: The Orsini family
entities.body: The Roman baronial family and its political and military following.

entities.name: The Colonna family
entities.body: The Roman baronial family and faction also called the Colonnesi.

entities.name: The Vitelli family
entities.body: The family of military commanders associated with Città di Castello.

entities.name: The Baglioni family
entities.body: The Perugian ruling family named among Cesare Borgia’s opponents.

entities.name: The Bentivoglio family
entities.body: The ruling family of Bologna, called the Bentivogli in this translation.

entities.name: The Sforza family
entities.body: The ruling dynasty of Milan established by Francesco Sforza.

entities.name: The Gracchi
entities.body: The Roman reforming brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, cited on reliance on popular support.

entities.name: The Canneschi
entities.body: The Bolognese family whose conspiracy targets Annibale Bentivoglio.

entities.name: The Cancellieri
entities.body: One of the rival Pistoian families named in the note on civil disorder.

entities.name: The Panciatichi
entities.body: One of the rival Pistoian families named in the note on civil disorder.

entities.name: The Bracceschi
entities.body: The soldiers and captains of Braccio’s military following.

entities.name: The Medici family
entities.body: The Florentine ruling family addressed in the final appeal to liberate Italy.

entities.name: The Marquess of Mantua
entities.body: The Mantuan ruler named among the Italian allies sought by Louis XII.

entities.name: The lords of the smaller Italian states
entities.body: The rulers of Faenza, Pesaro, Rimini, Camerino and Piombino who seek friendship with Louis XII.
